491.title: Forgive and have mercy
491.hook: my Lord, forgive and have mercy, You are the best of the merciful (23:118)
491.howItsDone: Many Muslims memorize 23:118 and repeat it as a short supplication, often counting it on their fingers or prayer beads after the daily prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: clay, drop, clot, bone, flesh, and then another creation. Your line was blessed is the best creator.

Some books save the best line for the last page. Al-Mu'minun does something like that. It opened, two days ago, with a bright promise: successful are the believers. Near its end, it goes somewhere dark. People who have died call out, my Lord, send me back, so that I might do right in what I left behind. And they're told it's only a word they're saying. Then the surah gathers itself, and its very last verse is a short prayer, handed to the Prophet ﷺ to say.

Verse one hundred eighteen. Pickthall: "And (O Muhammad) say: My Lord! Forgive and have mercy, for Thou art Best of all who show mercy." In Arabic: rabbi ghfir warham, wa anta khayru r-rahimin. Two verbs, ighfir and irham, and they aren't the same request. Ghafara has a sense of covering, of putting something over a fault so it no longer stands exposed. Rahma, mercy, is wider. It's the root of ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim in the bismillah, and many scholars connect it to rahim, the womb: care that surrounds you before you've done anything to earn it. So the prayer asks two things. Cover what I've done wrong. And hold me anyway. Then it gives the reason: You are the best of those who show mercy. Remember Ayyub, nine days ago, calling God the most merciful of the merciful. Different surah, close to the same title. And look where the line sits: right after the people who begged to be sent back. They asked for a second chance after it was too late. This verse is the version you say while there's still time. The surah's bookends are worth noticing too. It begins, qad aflaha l-mu'minun, successful are the believers. Just before this prayer, it says the deniers will not be successful, la yuflihu. Success at the start, its lack near the end, and between them, one short sentence anyone can carry.

If you don't pray, let ten breaths go by, and on each one think of something you'd like covered, and someone you'd like to be held.

492.title: Light upon light
492.hook: His light is like a niche with a lamp in glass like a shining star, lit from a blessed olive (24:35)
492.carry: neither of the east nor of the west
492.howItsDone: The Verse of Light, 24:35, is often recited and often appears in Islamic calligraphy; some medieval mosque lamps were inscribed with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rahma, the last line of Al-Mu'minun. Your line was best of the merciful.

Before electricity, a house at night had one or two small lights, and people knew them intimately. A clay lamp with a wick floating in olive oil. A little hollow cut into the wall to set it in, so the draft wouldn't catch it and the plaster would throw the light back into the room. Glass, if you were lucky, to make the flame burn steady and bright. Surah An-Nur, the Light, takes that ordinary lamp in the wall and uses it to describe something nobody can describe. Today, the Verse of Light.

It begins with a sentence almost too large: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth." Then, straight away, it gets small. The likeness of His light is a niche, a mishkat, and in it a lamp. The lamp is in a glass. The glass is like a shining star. The lamp is lit from a blessed tree, an olive, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow on its own, even if no fire touched it. Then the phrase this day is named for: "Light upon light." The picture is built in layers, and each one gathers the light and makes it brighter, until the verse runs out of images and simply says it: light on top of light. It ends by saying God guides to His light whom He wills, and sets out likenesses for people. It doesn't pretend the picture is the thing itself. It's a likeness, a way in. Commentators have read the layers in many ways: the believer's heart as the niche, the Qur'an as the oil, the Prophet as the lamp. The theologian al-Ghazali wrote a book on this verse, called The Niche of Lights. And the olive neither of the east nor of the west? Some say a tree standing in the open, catching sun all day. Others say it points beyond every direction. The verse leaves it open.
screen: `THE LIGHT OF THE HEAVENS AND EARTH.` · `NICHE, LAMP, GLASS, STAR.` · `OIL THAT ALMOST GLOWS.` · `LIGHT UPON LIGHT.`

segments.voice: If you can, switch on a small lamp or light a candle somewhere safe, and turn off the brighter lights around it; if not, look at whatever light is nearest, a window, a screen dimmed low. Watch how it falls on the wall behind it, and how the wall gives some of it back. If you pray, you can say the verse's opening line quietly.
Mishkat. The niche in the Verse of Light where the lamp sits, glowing through glass like a star.
Your line: neither of the east nor of the west. A likeness, and a way in. That's four hundred ninety-two.

493.title: Why didn't you think well?
493.hook: when you heard the slander, why didn't believers think good of their own (24:12)
493.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often cite 24:12 and the story of the slander, the ifk, when teaching about rumor and gossip, and encourage husn al-zann, thinking well of others, as an everyday habit.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mishkat, the niche in the Verse of Light. Your line was neither of the east nor of the west.
screen: `NEITHER OF THE EAST NOR OF THE WEST.`

segments.voice: An army is heading home through the desert. At one stop, a young woman steps away from camp, and on the way back finds her necklace is missing. She goes back to look for it. When she returns, the camp is gone; her litter was loaded onto the camel without anyone noticing she wasn't inside. She waits. A man who traveled behind the army finds her, lets her ride, and leads the camel back on foot. They arrive together, in daylight. Within hours, people are talking. The woman is 'A'isha, the Prophet's wife.

Bukhari preserves 'A'isha's own long account. The rumor spread through Medina for about a month. She fell ill and didn't know what was being said until a woman told her. She wept for two nights. Then verses of Surah An-Nur came down, declaring her innocent. And look at the first question those verses ask. Not, why did the slanderers lie? But this, in Pickthall's words: "Why did not the believers, men and women, when ye heard it, think good of their own folk, and say: It is a manifest untruth?" The question is aimed at the listeners: the ordinary people who heard it and passed it on, or just let it sit in their heads. A few verses later the surah describes how it happened: you took it up with your tongues, spoke with your mouths of what you had no knowledge of, and counted it a small thing, when with God it was great. That's how a rumor travels: it seems small. The word this day carries is husn al-zann, thinking well. Zann is an assumption, a guess about someone you can't fully see. Husn is goodness. So husn al-zann is choosing the good guess. A hadith in Bukhari gives the other side: beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the most false of talk. The surah doesn't ask people to be naive. It asks them to begin from good faith, especially about their own, and to say plainly when something is unproven. Think well first. The facts can come after.
screen: `'A'ISHA'S OWN ACCOUNT.` · `THE QUESTION IS FOR THE LISTENERS.` · `IT SEEMED SMALL; IT WAS GREAT.` · `HUSN AL-ZANN: CHOOSE THE GOOD GUESS.`

segments.voice: Think of one person whose behavior lately has bothered you, a late reply, a cold tone, a decision you didn't understand, and come up with three generous explanations: not excuses, just possibilities you can't rule out. Hold the kindest one for a while. If you pray, you can ask to think well of them.
Husn al-zann. Thinking well: choosing the good assumption about someone when you don't know the whole story. Today's word.
Your line: think well first. A rumor can stop with you, and the facts can wait. See you tomorrow.

494.title: Lower the gaze
494.hook: believing men and women are both told to lower their gaze and guard their modesty (24:30–31)
494.howItsDone: Many Muslims understand lowering the gaze as avoiding lingering or immodest looks, for men and women alike, and some extend it to what they choose to watch online.

segments.voice: Yesterday: husn al-zann, choosing the good guess. Your line was think well first.

A face across the train car. A stranger's phone screen, lit up and readable. A photo that stops the thumb mid-scroll. The eyes move first, before anyone has decided anything, and then they linger. Advertisers know this, and so does every app built to keep a thumb scrolling. Surah An-Nur gives a short instruction about the eyes. It is often remembered as a rule for women alone. Look at who hears it first.

Verse thirty. Pickthall: "Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and be modest." Men first. Then the next verse turns to women with the same opening: "And tell the believing women to lower their gaze and be modest". Same verbs, same duty. The verse to women goes on with more detail about dress, and scholars have written a great deal about that. But the gaze comes first, and it's shared. The Arabic is yaghuddu min absarihim. Ghadd means to lower, to lessen, the way you'd lower your voice. And the little word min, from, matters. Some commentators read it as: lower some of your gaze. Not shut your eyes, not walk around staring at your shoes. You still see the person you're talking to. What gets lowered is the lingering, the second look that turns into staring. A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi makes the same point. The Prophet ﷺ told 'Ali: don't follow one glance with another. The first is yours; the second is not. The first look just happens. The second is a choice. And it isn't only about attraction. In a hadith in Bukhari, the Prophet listed the rights of the road for people who sit by the street, and lowering the gaze is the first of them. Next to it: not harming anyone, returning greetings, encouraging good. So guarding the eyes is also manners: not staring into the neighbor's open door, not reading a stranger's messages over their shoulder, not lingering on someone who'd rather not be looked at.
screen: `MEN ADDRESSED FIRST.` · `GHADD: LOWER, LESSEN.` · `THE FIRST LOOK IS YOURS.` · `A RIGHT OF THE ROAD.`

495.title: Knock and greet
495.hook: don't enter houses until you've asked permission and greeted the people (24:27)
495.tomorrow: Don't you want to be forgiven?
495.howItsDone: Muslim families often teach children to knock, say as-salamu 'alaykum and wait before entering a room, following 24:27–28 and the hadith on asking permission three times.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ghadd al-basar, lowering the gaze. Your line was guard the eyes.

Commentators on this verse describe an older habit. A visitor would walk straight into a house and call out a greeting once already inside, good morning, to someone who might not be ready to be seen. Sometimes a curtain was all that stood in the way. Surah An-Nur, a surah full of rules about privacy and dignity, sets down a small one about thresholds. It's so ordinary you could miss how much it says.

Verse twenty-seven. Pickthall begins: "O ye who believe! Enter not houses other than your own". Not until you've made yourselves known, and greeted the people inside with peace. The verb for making yourself known is tasta'nisu. Commentators link it to uns, the word for ease, friendliness, feeling at home with someone. So it isn't only asking permission. It's waiting until the people inside are comfortable with you being there. The next verse adds: if you find no one at home, don't go in. And if you're told to go back, go back; that is purer for you. No argument, no peering through the window. The hadith fill in the picture. Bukhari records Abu Musa going to 'Umar's house, asking permission three times, getting no answer, and leaving. When 'Umar later asked why he'd left, Abu Musa said the Prophet ﷺ taught: ask permission three times, and if you're not given it, go back. Another report, in Abu Dawud, says that when the Prophet came to someone's door, he would stand to one side of it, not facing straight in, and give the greeting. That's the whole lesson in a posture: stand where you can't see in, say peace, wait. So knock and greet isn't fussy etiquette. It's respect for another person's space, the part of their life they get to decide about. Today doors have locks and houses have bells, but the same idea reaches a bedroom door, a phone left on a table, a message thread that isn't yours.

496.title: Don't you want to be forgiven?
496.hook: Abu Bakr forgives a relative who spread the slander after this verse: pardon and overlook (24:22)
496.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often tell the story of Abu Bakr and Mistah with 24:22 when speaking about forgiveness within families, and many Muslims recall its question when they find it hard to let go of a grievance.

segments.voice: Yesterday: uns, the ease a visitor waits for at the door. Your line was ask before entering.

Three days ago, the rumor about 'A'isha. Now the other side of it. Her father, Abu Bakr, had a poor relative named Mistah, a cousin's son, and for years Abu Bakr had paid for his keep. When the slander spread, Mistah was one of the people repeating it, about his own benefactor's daughter. After the verses came down clearing her, Abu Bakr swore an oath: he would never spend on Mistah again. Plenty of people would call that fair. Then another verse came down.

Verse twenty-two speaks to people of means who swear not to give to their relatives, the poor, and those who emigrated for God's sake. Mistah was all three. Then, in Pickthall's words: "Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you?" Two verbs again. Ya'fu: to pardon, to let the debt go. Yasfahu: to overlook, to turn away from it, to stop bringing it up. Scholars often describe the second as one step further than the first: not only letting the wrong go, but not holding it over the person afterward. And then the question. Not a command, a question: don't you want God to forgive you? 'A'isha's account in Bukhari says that when Abu Bakr heard this, he said: yes, by God, I want God to forgive me. He went back to supporting Mistah, and said he would never stop. Look at what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say Mistah was right. It doesn't say the harm was small; the verses before called it great. It doesn't ask Abu Bakr to trust Mistah with secrets. It asks him not to cut off the support that kept a poor relative fed. Pardon isn't pretending it didn't happen, and it isn't letting someone keep hurting you. It's refusing to make the rest of the relationship pay for one wound. And the reason it gives is personal: everyone needs forgiving for something.
screen: `AN OATH TO STOP GIVING.` · `PARDON, AND OVERLOOK.` · `DON'T YOU WANT TO BE FORGIVEN?` · `YES, BY GOD. THE SUPPORT RESUMES.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who hurt you in a modest way, a careless word, a broken promise, a snub; not the deepest wound, and not anyone who is still harming you. Notice what you've been holding back from them because of it, and ask yourself the verse's question, gently. If you pray, you can ask to be able to let it go, and to be forgiven too.
Mistah. The poor relative who spread the rumor about 'A'isha, and whom Abu Bakr chose to keep supporting anyway. Today's word.
Your line: pardon, and be pardoned. Pardon never means letting someone keep hurting you. Day four hundred ninety-six, done.

497.title: The criterion
497.hook: the book that separates right from wrong (25:1)
497.howItsDone: Muslims use al-Furqan as one of the names of the Qur'an, alongside al-Kitab and adh-Dhikr, and teachers cite 8:29 when speaking of the clarity that comes with mindfulness of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mistah, and the question, don't you want to be forgiven? Your line was pardon, and be pardoned. Today ends the week.

A ship's compass doesn't tell you where you want to go. It doesn't make the decision. It does one thing: it shows which way north is, so every other choice can be measured against it. Without it, at night, in fog, all directions feel the same. Surah Al-Furqan opens by giving the Qur'an a name that works a little like that. Not the book, not the reading. A name that means: the thing that tells two things apart.

Pickthall: "Blessed is He Who hath revealed unto His slave the Criterion (of right and wrong), that he may be a warner to the peoples." The Criterion is al-furqan. Its root, f-r-q, means to separate, to part, to make a distinction. Faraqa: he divided. Firqa: a group that has split off. Furqan is the thing that divides: true from false, right from wrong, the path from the drift. Pickthall's brackets say what the criterion tells apart. And the word isn't used only for this book. The Qur'an says Musa and Harun were given al-furqan too. It calls the day of the battle of Badr yawm al-furqan, the day of distinction, when two sides met and the difference between them became plain. And in Surah Al-Anfal there's a promise: if you are mindful of God, He will give you a furqan. That one is inside a person: a sense of the difference, sharpened by taqwa, that helps you see which way to go when the options blur. Tradition gives 'Umar ibn al-Khattab the title al-Faruq, the one who distinguishes, for how clearly he drew that line. So furqan works on three levels: a book, a day, and a faculty inside you. This week was full of differences: light and dark, the rumor and the good assumption, the first look and the second, walking in and knocking, the oath and the pardon. Furqan is the name for the thing that tells them apart.

Furqan. The criterion, the thing that tells right from wrong: a name for the Qur'an, for the day of Badr, and for a clarity inside a mindful person. Today's word.
Your line: tell right from wrong. A book, a day, and a clarity inside you. That's the week.
